body_en:
When you become an Australian citizen, you make a pledge of loyalty to Australia and its people. The booklet says this is why it matters to understand the community you are joining, including its Indigenous heritage, and how Australia grew into the stable and successful multicultural nation it is today.

Part 1 of the booklet begins with that heritage. Australia's first inhabitants are the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Their cultures and traditions are the oldest continuous cultures anywhere in the world, and they are still living cultures, not something that belongs only to the past.

The booklet distinguishes two groups. Aboriginal people have their historical home on the mainland and in Tasmania. Torres Strait Islander people come from the islands scattered between Queensland's northern tip and Papua New Guinea. The archaeological record suggests Aboriginal peoples have been in Australia for somewhere between forty thousand and sixty-five thousand years.

Aboriginal peoples themselves understand their story differently: they see themselves as central to the creation stories of this land, and those stories begin with the beginning of time. Age-old beliefs and traditions continue to guide Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples today. A deep connection with the land sits at the heart of these cultures, and it is expressed through stories, through art and through dance.

The booklet also stresses that Indigenous cultures are not one single culture. They are diverse, with many different peoples and traditions across the continent and the islands, and together they form an important part of Australia's national identity. Language is one sign of that diversity. English is Australia's national language, but the booklet says other languages are valued too, and it points out that there are more than one hundred distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages.

The glossary at the end of the testable section defines the word Indigenous as meaning the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples of Australia, and describes Indigenous Australians as the First Peoples of this country. For the test, the points to remember are simple. Know who the first inhabitants are, know that their cultures are the oldest continuous cultures in the world, know which group comes from the mainland and Tasmania and which from the islands north of Queensland, and know that connection to land is expressed through stories, art and dance. Remember too that these cultures are diverse and are part of what makes Australia the nation it is.
keyFacts_en: Australia's first inhabitants are the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Their cultures and traditions are the oldest continuous cultures in the world.
Aboriginal people are historically from mainland Australia and Tasmania.
Torres Strait Islander people are from islands between the northern tip of Queensland and Papua New Guinea.
Their deep connection with the land is expressed through stories, art and dance.
Indigenous cultures are diverse and an important part of Australia's national identity.
More than 100 distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages are valued alongside English.
The glossary describes Indigenous Australians as the First Peoples of this country.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia and its people; Part 1 — Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples; Part 1 — The nation of Australia; Glossary of testable section

title_en: Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country
body_en:
Two protocols appear often at Australian events, and the test regularly asks about them, so it is worth being clear about how they differ. The first is a Welcome to Country. This is a cultural practice carried out by an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian of the local region.

The custodian welcomes visitors onto their traditional land. Historically the practice had a practical purpose: it was performed so that visitors would have a safe and protected journey while they were on that land. A Welcome to Country does not have one fixed form. It may be a song, a dance, a smoking ceremony, or a speech, and a speech can be given in a traditional language or in English.

When it is part of an event, it is normally the very first item of proceedings, because its role is to open the event. The key point for the test is who performs it. Only an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian of the local region gives a Welcome to Country. The organiser, the Master of Ceremonies or a person who simply lives in the area cannot do it.

The second protocol is an Acknowledgement of Country. This is an opportunity to recognise that the gathering is taking place on Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander land, to pay respect to the Traditional Custodians, particularly Elders past and present, and to pay respect to any Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people who are present. Unlike a Welcome, an Acknowledgement of Country can be delivered by anyone.

At meetings and events it is usually part of the Welcome and Housekeeping at the beginning, and it is generally given by the Chair or the Master of Ceremonies. The booklet sums up the purpose of both practices in one idea: both exist to show respect to Australia's First Peoples.

You may experience this yourself. The booklet's description of the citizenship ceremony notes that you may be welcomed by a representative of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people who are the traditional owners of the land in your area, following the Welcome to Country protocol. A simple way to keep the two apart is to think about the word itself.

A Welcome is given by the people whose land it is, and only they can offer it. An Acknowledgement is given by anyone else, recognising whose land it is. Both open an event, both show respect, and only one of them is restricted in who may perform it.
keyFacts_en: A Welcome to Country is performed by an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander custodian of the local region.
It welcomes visitors to the custodians' traditional land and was traditionally meant to give visitors a safe and protected journey.
A Welcome to Country can be a song, a dance, a smoking ceremony or a speech in traditional language or English.
A Welcome to Country is usually the first item of proceedings at an event.
An Acknowledgement of Country recognises the gathering is on Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander land and pays respect to Traditional Custodians and Elders.
Anyone can deliver an Acknowledgement of Country, usually the Chair or Master of Ceremonies during the Welcome and Housekeeping.
Both practices are performed to show respect for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
At a citizenship ceremony you may be welcomed by a representative of the traditional owners of the land in your area.
guideRef: Part 1 — Traditions — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols; A message to you — The Australian citizenship ceremony

body_en:
The story of modern Australia as the booklet tells it begins on 26 January 1788. That is the date the First Fleet arrived from Great Britain, and it is the moment the booklet uses to mark the start of European settlement. The anniversary of that arrival is still celebrated every year as Australia Day.

In the decades that followed, free settlers came to the new colonies, and they came mainly from Great Britain and Ireland. The booklet makes a point of this British and Irish heritage because it has had a major influence on Australia's recent history, on its culture and on its politics. Over time more colonies were set up in other parts of the continent.

The next date to remember is 1901. In that year the separate colonies agreed to unite into a federation of states, and the new nation was named the Commonwealth of Australia. The glossary defines Federation as the union of colonies into one nation, with the colonies keeping certain powers of their own. Federation was also the moment Australia's national democratic institutions were created.

The national parliament, the national government and the High Court were all established under the new Australian Constitution in 1901. One further date matters. For many decades, official estimates of the population left out Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. That changed only after a Referendum held in 1967, after which they were included in the official figures.

The booklet then turns to how Australia's population has changed. More recently, migrants and refugees have arrived from every part of the world. Their reasons vary: reuniting with family, starting afresh, or getting away from poverty, war or persecution. Over the last two centuries the diversity of the population has grown, and the booklet describes this diverse and prosperous society as something that strengthens Australia's connection with the rest of the world.

At the same time, Australia aims to be a cohesive and unified nation, not just a collection of separate communities. Language is part of that unity. English is the national language and part of the national identity. The booklet says migrants should learn and use English because it helps them take part in Australian society and make the most of living and working here.

Other languages are valued as well, and the booklet points out that there are more than one hundred distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages. For the test, hold on to the three dates, the British and Irish heritage, the name of the nation formed in 1901, the role of English, and the idea of diversity within a unified nation.
keyFacts_en: European settlement began when the First Fleet arrived from Great Britain on 26 January 1788.
Early free settlers came from Great Britain and Ireland, and this heritage has shaped Australia's history, culture and politics.
In 1901 the colonies united into a federation of states called the Commonwealth of Australia.
The national parliament, government and High Court were established under the Constitution at Federation.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples were included in official population estimates only after the 1967 Referendum.
Australia's national language is English, and migrants should learn and use it to take part in society.
More than 100 distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages are also valued.
Australia celebrates its diversity while aiming to build a cohesive and unified nation.
guideRef: Part 1 — Early days of European settlement; Part 1 — The nation of Australia; Glossary of testable section

title_en: The six states and their capitals
body_en:
Australia is a federation, and it is made up of six states together with two mainland territories. Canberra is the national capital, and each state and mainland territory also has a capital city of its own. Questions about capitals are among the most commonly reported on the real test, so learn all of them. The six states and their capitals are New South Wales with Sydney, Victoria with Melbourne, Queensland with Brisbane, Western Australia with Perth, South Australia with Adelaide, and Tasmania with Hobart.

The booklet then gives a short portrait of each state. New South Wales was the first colony the British established. Its capital, Sydney, is the largest city in the nation, and two of its landmarks, the Sydney Harbour Bridge and the Opera House, are national icons. The glossary explains that an icon is a well-known image, and it uses the Opera House as its example.

Of the states on the mainland, Victoria is the smallest. Three Victorian icons to remember are the Melbourne Cricket Ground, the 12 Apostles and the Royal Exhibition Building. Queensland comes second in size among the states. The Torres Strait Islands lie to its north, and the Great Barrier Reef, famous around the world, runs along its eastern coast. Queensland's landscape ranges from tropical rainforest to temperate coast to an inland that is often dry.

The largest state of all is Western Australia. Much of its east is desert, while the south-west is a rich farming and wine-growing region, and the state hosts many large mining projects. Its icons are the Ningaloo Coast, Margaret River and the Kimberley region.

South Australia is known for a rugged coast and for its many celebrated wine regions. Adelaide is noted for its fine colonial architecture, and the state's icons include the Barossa Valley and the Flinders Ranges. Tasmania is the smallest state and the only one that is an island, separated from the mainland by the Bass Strait. Much of it is unspoilt wilderness, and its icons include Cradle Mountain, Port Arthur and the Bay of Fires.

Two distinctions trip people up. Tasmania is the smallest state overall, while Victoria is the smallest of the mainland states. Western Australia is the largest state, and Queensland is the second largest. If you can match each capital to its state and each set of icons to its state, and you remember which states are largest and smallest, you will be well prepared for this part of the test.
keyFacts_en: Australia has six states and two mainland territories, and Canberra is the national capital.
The state capitals are Sydney (NSW), Melbourne (Victoria), Brisbane (Queensland), Perth (WA), Adelaide (SA) and Hobart (Tasmania).
New South Wales was the first British colony, and Sydney is the nation's largest city.
Victoria is the smallest mainland state; Tasmania, separated by the Bass Strait, is the smallest state overall.
Western Australia is the largest state and Queensland is the second largest.
The Great Barrier Reef runs along Queensland's eastern coast.
Each state has its own icons, such as the Barossa Valley in South Australia and Cradle Mountain in Tasmania.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories; Part 1 — The states; Glossary of testable section

body_en:
Alongside the six states, Australia has two mainland territories, and the booklet treats them separately. The first is the Australian Capital Territory, usually shortened to the ACT. It sits between Sydney and Melbourne, and it exists to house the national capital, Canberra.

Canberra is therefore both the capital of the ACT and the capital of the whole country. Because it is the seat of national government, several national institutions are located there. The booklet names two in particular: Parliament House, where the national parliament meets, and the High Court of Australia.

When a test question asks for Australia's capital, the answer is Canberra, not Sydney or Melbourne, even though those cities are larger and better known overseas. The second mainland territory is the Northern Territory, whose capital is Darwin. The territory stretches across very different landscapes.

In the north the environment is tropical, while the south is dry red desert. Its icons are some of the most recognisable places in Australia: Uluru, Kata Tjuta and Kings Canyon. It helps to keep the full list of eight capitals together in your mind. The six state capitals are Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth, Adelaide and Hobart.

The two territory capitals are Canberra for the Australian Capital Territory and Darwin for the Northern Territory. A common mistake is to confuse a territory with a state. Tasmania and Queensland are states; the Northern Territory and the Australian Capital Territory are territories. The booklet describes the Commonwealth of Australia as a federation of states and territories, so both kinds of unit are part of the nation, but when a question asks how many states there are, the answer is six, and when it asks about mainland territories, the answer is two.

Another useful habit is to attach each territory to its most distinctive features. For the ACT, think of national institutions and its location between Sydney and Melbourne. For the Northern Territory, think of Darwin in the tropical north, red desert in the south, and Uluru. Those associations make it easy to answer questions that approach the same facts from different directions, whether they ask for a capital, a location, a landscape or an icon.
keyFacts_en: Australia's two mainland territories are the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory.
The Australian Capital Territory lies between Sydney and Melbourne and is home to Canberra, the national capital.
Parliament House and the High Court of Australia are among the national institutions in Canberra.
Darwin is the capital of the Northern Territory.
The Northern Territory is tropical in the north and dry red desert in the south.
Uluru, Kata Tjuta and Kings Canyon are Northern Territory icons.
Tasmania and Queensland are states, while the Northern Territory and the ACT are territories.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's states and territories; Part 1 — The territories

body_en:
The booklet singles out two days in the year as especially important for Australians, and both appear regularly in the test. The first is Australia Day, celebrated on 26 January. It is a public holiday in every state and territory, and the booklet calls it the biggest annual public holiday in the country. The date was chosen because the First Fleet from Great Britain reached Australia on that day in 1788.

On Australia Day, communities around the country think about Australia's history and about the people who have contributed to the achievements the nation shares. The booklet frames the day as a celebration of the contribution of every Australian, from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, who have been here for about sixty-five thousand years, to families who have lived here for generations, to people who have arrived recently from every part of the world.

Events are held across the country, and many of them are citizenship ceremonies, so the day has a special meaning for new citizens. One detail to remember is that the Australian of the Year Awards are announced in Canberra by the Prime Minister as part of the celebrations.

The second important day is Anzac Day, commemorated on 25 April. Its mood is very different. The name comes from the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, which landed at Gallipoli in Türkiye on 25 April 1915, during World War I.

Anzac Day is a solemn day of remembrance. Australians remember the sacrifice of everyone who served and died in wars, in conflicts and in peacekeeping operations. It is also a day to honour the courage and commitment shown by servicemen and women, and to think about what war has meant in its many different ways. A simple way to keep the two days apart is to remember that Australia Day is a celebration and Anzac Day is a remembrance.

One looks back to the beginning of European settlement, the other looks back to the landing at Gallipoli. The practice test has asked what Australians remember on Anzac Day, and the answer is all those who have fought and died in wars, not the creation of the nation and not the arrival of the First Fleet. Make sure you can give the date of each day, the event each one marks, and the way each one is observed.
keyFacts_en: Australia Day is celebrated on 26 January and is a public holiday in every state and territory.
Australia Day is the anniversary of the First Fleet's arrival from Great Britain in 1788 and is the biggest annual public holiday.
Australia Day events include special citizenship ceremonies, and the Prime Minister announces the Australian of the Year Awards in Canberra.
Anzac Day is commemorated on 25 April.
Anzac stands for the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, which landed at Gallipoli in Türkiye on 25 April 1915 during World War I.
Anzac Day is a solemn day remembering all Australians who served and died in wars, conflicts and peacekeeping operations.
On Anzac Day Australians also honour the courage and commitment of all servicemen and women.
guideRef: Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Australia Day; Part 1 — Important days for Australians — Anzac Day

body_en:
Australia has one official national flag, and two other flags that are officially recognised and may be flown in the community: the Australian Aboriginal Flag and the Torres Strait Islander Flag. Each state and territory has its own flag as well. The test often asks about the colours of the flags and what their parts stand for, so it is worth learning each one element by element. The national flag uses three colours: blue, white and red.

In the top left corner is the Union Jack, the flag of the United Kingdom. It stands for Australia's history of British settlement and the laws and institutions that came with it. Below the Union Jack is the Commonwealth Star. This star has seven points. Six of them represent the six states, and the seventh represents the territories.

On the right-hand side of the flag is the Southern Cross, a group of stars that can be seen in the southern sky. The Aboriginal Flag has three colours, black, red and yellow, each with a meaning. Its black upper half stands for the Aboriginal peoples of Australia. Its red lower half stands for the earth, which carries ceremonial significance.

The yellow circle in the middle is the sun. Four colours make up the Torres Strait Islander Flag: green, blue, black and white. The green stripes at the top and bottom represent the land. The central blue panel stands for the sea. The thin black lines stand for the Torres Strait Islander people themselves.

In the middle is a white dancer's headdress, a symbol for all Torres Strait Islanders, and inside it is a white star. Each point of the star stands for one of the island groups of the Torres Strait, and white is the colour of peace.

Because two of the flags carry a star, it is easy to mix them up. The Commonwealth Star on the national flag has seven points for the states and territories. The white star on the Torres Strait Islander Flag has points for the island groups.

In the same way, both the Aboriginal Flag and the Torres Strait Islander Flag use black to represent people, but the Aboriginal Flag uses a yellow circle for the sun and red for the earth, while the Torres Strait Islander Flag uses green for land and blue for sea. If you can name the colours of each flag and say what each colour or shape stands for, you will be ready for almost any flag question the test can ask.
keyFacts_en: The Australian National Flag is the official flag; the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander flags are also officially recognised.
The national flag is blue, white and red, with the Union Jack in the top left corner representing British settlement and inherited laws and institutions.
The Commonwealth Star under the Union Jack has seven points: six for the states and one for the territories.
The Southern Cross on the right of the national flag is a group of stars seen in the southern sky.
The Aboriginal Flag is black, red and yellow: black for the Aboriginal peoples, red for the earth, and a yellow circle for the sun.
The Torres Strait Islander Flag is green, blue, black and white: green for land, blue for sea, black lines for the people.
The white dancer's headdress is a symbol for all Torres Strait Islanders; the star's points are the island groups and white means peace.
Each state and territory also has its own flag.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's flags

title_en: Coat of Arms, national emblems and anthem
body_en:
Beyond the flags, the booklet describes a set of national symbols that identify Australia, and several of them are favourite subjects for test questions. Australia's official national symbol is the Commonwealth Coat of Arms. It represents national unity, and it is used to identify the authority and the property of the Commonwealth.

In the centre is a shield that represents the six states and their federation. On either side of the shield stand two native Australian animals, a kangaroo and an emu, holding it up. Above the shield sits a gold Commonwealth Star, the same seven-pointed star that appears on the national flag.

Behind everything is a background of golden wattle. The golden wattle is Australia's national flower. It is a small tree found mainly in south-eastern Australia, with bright green leaves and masses of golden yellow flowers that appear in spring. The glossary uses the term floral emblem to mean national flower, and each state and territory has a floral emblem of its own.

The wattle also explains Australia's national colours. They are green and gold, the colours of the golden wattle, and that is why the uniforms of Australia's national sporting teams are usually green and gold. Australia's national gemstone is the opal.

The booklet also records an Aboriginal legend about the opal: its colours were created when a rainbow came down and touched the earth. Candidates often report being asked for the national flower, the national colours and the national gemstone, so these three are worth committing firmly to memory: golden wattle, green and gold, and opal.

The last symbol is the national anthem. Australia's national anthem is Advance Australia Fair. The glossary defines a national anthem simply as a national song. It is sung on occasions of national importance, including citizenship ceremonies and major sporting events, and the booklet notes that at your own citizenship ceremony everyone present will sing it.

The anthem opens with the words Australians all let us rejoice, for we are one and free, and its second verse welcomes those who have come across the seas. Learning the first line is useful, because it is the part of the anthem the test is most likely to ask about. Taken together, the Coat of Arms, the wattle, the national colours, the opal and the anthem are the images and sounds that Australians use to represent their country to themselves and to the world.
keyFacts_en: The Commonwealth Coat of Arms is the official symbol of the Commonwealth of Australia and represents national unity.
On the Coat of Arms the shield represents the six states and federation, a kangaroo and an emu support it, and a gold Commonwealth Star sits above it.
The background of the Coat of Arms is the golden wattle, Australia's national flower, which grows mainly in south-eastern Australia.
Australia's national colours are green and gold, the colours of the golden wattle, and national sports teams usually wear them.
The opal is Australia's national gemstone; legend says a rainbow touched the earth and created its colours.
Advance Australia Fair is the national anthem, sung at citizenship ceremonies and major sporting events.
The anthem's first line is Australians all let us rejoice, for we are one and free.
In the glossary, floral emblem means national flower and national anthem means national song.
guideRef: Part 1 — Australia's symbols; Part 1 — Australia's national anthem; A message to you — The Australian citizenship ceremony; Glossary of testable section

body_en:
When you take the pledge at your citizenship ceremony, you promise to share Australia's democratic beliefs and to respect its rights and liberties. Part 2 of the booklet sets out what those beliefs are, and the test treats them as essential knowledge.

The first belief is parliamentary democracy. Australia's system of government is a parliamentary democracy, which the glossary defines as a system based on citizens regularly electing representatives to parliament. The important idea is where power comes from. The government's power comes from the Australian people, because citizens vote for the people who represent them in parliament.

At election time those representatives have to account to voters for what they have decided. If voters are unhappy, the remedy is the ballot box, not force. The second belief is the Rule of Law. All Australians are equal under the law, and no person, group or religious rule is above it.

Everyone must obey Australia's laws, including people who hold positions of power: government leaders, community leaders, religious leaders, business people and the police. The glossary makes the point sharply by saying that even the Prime Minister is bound by the law.

The third belief is living peacefully. Australians take pride in living in a peaceful country whose system of government is stable. They believe that change should happen through discussion, peaceful persuasion and the democratic process, and they reject violence as a way to change a person's mind or to change the law. Several test questions are built on this idea, usually as a short scenario asking whether some violent or threatening act is acceptable. The answer the booklet gives is always that it is not.

The fourth belief is respect for every individual regardless of background. The democratic system rests on the idea that each person, no matter where they come from, enjoys rights and equal standing under Australian law. Everyone is expected to treat others with dignity and respect, and the booklet gives a long list of differences that must make no difference: race, country of origin, gender, sexual orientation, marital status, age, disability, heritage, culture, politics, wealth and religion.

The glossary defines respect as showing consideration for someone as a person, or for a decision they have made, and it defines democracy as government by the people through elected representatives. If you keep these four beliefs in mind, parliamentary democracy, the Rule of Law, living peacefully and respect for all, you can answer most questions in this section by asking which option fits them.
keyFacts_en: At the citizenship ceremony you pledge to share Australia's democratic beliefs and respect its rights and liberties.
Australia is a parliamentary democracy: citizens vote for representatives, and government power comes from the people.
Representatives in parliament answer to the people through elections for the decisions they make.
Under the Rule of Law, all Australians are equal under the law and no person, group or religious rule is above it.
Everyone must obey the law, including government, community and religious leaders, business people, the police and the Prime Minister.
Australians believe change should come through discussion, peaceful persuasion and the democratic process, and reject violence.
Every individual has rights and equality under the law, and all Australians are expected to treat each other with dignity and respect regardless of background.
guideRef: Part 2 — Australia's democratic beliefs, rights and liberties; Part 2 — Our democratic beliefs; Glossary of testable section

title_en: Our equalities and the fair go
body_en:
The second half of Part 2 of the booklet is about equality, and the real test is known to ask about it, especially the equal rights of men and women. The starting point is that Australia has a number of laws that make sure a person is not treated differently from others because of their gender, their race, a disability or their age. These laws turn the general belief in equality into something enforceable.

The booklet then gives two examples. The first is gender equality. Men and women have equal rights in Australia, and it is against the law to discriminate against a person because of their gender.

In practice this means an employer cannot refuse someone a job because they are a woman, and a woman has the same right as a man to take part in public life, including standing for parliament. If a test question offers a choice between men having more rights, women having more rights, or men and women having equal rights, the booklet's answer is that their rights are equal.

The second example is equality of opportunity, which Australians often call a fair go. The idea is that what a person achieves in life should be the result of their talents, their work and their effort, not of their wealth or their background. The glossary describes a fair go as everyone, regardless of background, being given an equal opportunity to achieve success in life. The booklet links this to the kind of society Australia wants to be: equal opportunity is meant to make sure there are no formal class distinctions in Australian society.

Someone from a poor family who works hard and succeeds is a good illustration of a fair go in action, and a job going to the best candidate rather than the best-connected one is another. The glossary also gives a short definition of equality itself as being the same in status, and it lists Australia's liberties as freedom of speech, freedom of expression, freedom of religion and freedom of association.

Those freedoms are explained in detail in the next chapter, but it helps to know that the booklet groups them together under the single word liberties, because a question may use that word. To prepare for this section, remember three things: laws protect people from being treated differently because of gender, race, disability or age; men and women have equal rights and gender discrimination is illegal; and a fair go means opportunity based on talent, work and effort rather than wealth or background, in a society with no formal class distinctions.
keyFacts_en: Australian laws ensure a person is not treated differently because of their gender, race, disability or age.
Men and women have equal rights in Australia.
It is against the law to discriminate against a person because of their gender.
Australians value equal opportunity, often called a fair go.
A fair go means achievement should come from talents, work and effort rather than wealth or background.
Equality of opportunity is meant to ensure there are no formal class distinctions in Australian society.
The glossary defines equality as the same in status and lists liberties as freedom of speech, expression, religion and association.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our equalities; Glossary of testable section

title_en: Freedom of speech, expression and association
body_en:
Part 2 of the booklet describes the freedoms Australians share, and the glossary calls them liberties, meaning personal freedom and independence. The first is freedom of speech, which the booklet calls a core Australian value that underpins the democratic system.

In practice it means people may say and write what they believe and talk their ideas over with others. The booklet gives concrete examples: people can criticise the government, protest peacefully against government decisions and campaign to change laws. There is one condition attached to every example, and it is the condition the test most often checks. People must obey Australian law at all times, even while exercising their freedom of speech.

Freedom of expression is closely related. It means people can express their views through art, film, music and literature, not only through words. People may also gather, whether in a public place or a private one, to talk about social or political matters. Again the law must be obeyed throughout, and the booklet adds a second duty: we must respect other people's freedom of speech and expression too.

A view you dislike is still a view the other person is free to hold and to express. The second freedom in this lesson is freedom of association. It is the right to set up groups, and to join them, in order to work towards shared goals.

In Australia people are free to join any legal organisation, and the booklet lists political parties, trade unions, and religious, cultural and social groups as examples. The right works in both directions. People can decide not to join an organisation, and nobody can be forced into joining one.

Australians may also come together to protest, whether the target is something the government has done or the conduct of an organisation. The same condition applies as before: the laws of Australia must be obeyed, so a gathering must be peaceful, and it must not injure any person or damage any property.

When a test question describes a scenario, ask two things. First, is the activity a form of speech, expression or association, such as criticising the government, making a film, joining a union or meeting friends to talk about politics? If so, it is allowed. Second, does the scenario involve breaking the law, for example through violence, threats or damage to property?

If so, the freedom does not excuse it. Keeping those two questions in mind will carry you through almost every item on this section, because every freedom the booklet describes comes paired with the same duty to obey the law and to respect the same freedom in others.
keyFacts_en: Freedom of speech is a core Australian value and underpins the democratic system.
Freedom of speech means people can say and write what they think, criticise the government, protest peacefully and campaign to change laws.
Freedom of expression means people can express their views through art, film, music and literature.
People are free to meet in public or private places for social or political discussion.
Australian laws must be obeyed at all times, and other people's freedom of speech and expression must be respected.
Freedom of association is the right to form and join associations, such as political parties, trade unions, and religious, cultural or social groups.
People can decide not to join an organisation and cannot be forced to join.
Protest gatherings must be peaceful and must not injure anyone or damage property.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of speech and freedom of expression; Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of association; Glossary of testable section

title_en: Freedom of religion and the secular state
body_en:
The third freedom described in Part 2 of the booklet is freedom of religion, and it comes with an important idea about how government works in Australia. The booklet begins with heritage. Australia's heritage is Judaeo-Christian and many Australians call themselves Christians, yet followers of all the world's large religions live here. That heritage shows in the calendar, because Australia has public holidays on Christian days such as Good Friday, Easter Sunday and Christmas Day.

Heritage, however, does not mean preference in law. Every citizen is treated the same by the government and by the law, no matter what they believe. The government in Australia is secular. The glossary defines secular as separate from religion, and the booklet explains that a secular government operates separately from churches and other religious entities.

There is no official national religion in Australia. The official practice test asks about this directly, and the correct idea is that the government is separate from any religion; it does not tell people which religion to follow and it does not base its laws on an official religion.

Within that framework, people are free to follow any religion they choose, and they are equally free to follow no religion at all. A migrant may keep practising the faith of their home country, a person may change their beliefs, and a person may decide that religion plays no part in their life.

All of these are free choices in Australia. The booklet attaches the same condition to religion that it attaches to the other freedoms. Religious practice does not suspend the law: Australian laws must be followed at all times, including during worship. It then goes one step further and answers the question of what happens when the two collide.

If a religious practice and an Australian law point in different directions, it is the Australian law that wins. This is one of the ideas the test treats as a matter of values, so make sure you understand it rather than just remembering the words.

Freedom of religion protects the right to believe and to worship, but it does not place any religious rule above the law of the land, which fits with the Rule of Law described earlier in Part 2. To summarise, remember that Australia has a Judaeo-Christian heritage and Christian public holidays, that the government is secular with no official national religion, that every person is free to follow any religion or none and is treated equally by the law, and that when religious practice and Australian law conflict, the law comes first.
keyFacts_en: Australia has a Judaeo-Christian heritage, and people from all the large religions live in Australia.
Good Friday, Easter Sunday and Christmas Day are public holidays.
The government and the law treat all citizens equally, whatever their religion or beliefs.
The government is secular, meaning it operates separately from churches and other religious bodies, and Australia has no official national religion.
People are free to follow any religion they choose, or to follow no religion.
Australian laws must be obeyed at all times, even while engaging in religious practices.
Where an Australian law conflicts with a religious practice, Australian law prevails.
In the glossary, secular means separate from religion and liberty means personal freedom and independence.
guideRef: Part 2 — Our freedoms — Freedom of religion; Glossary of testable section

body_en:
Becoming an Australian citizen changes your relationship with the country. Part 2 of the booklet describes this as a two-way bond. On one side are responsibilities, the things you will give Australia. On the other side are privileges, the things Australia will give you. This lesson covers the responsibilities. There are four of them, and the test often checks that you can tell a responsibility apart from a privilege.

The first responsibility is to obey the law. Laws are made by the representatives we elect so that society stays orderly, free and safe, and so that everyone's rights are protected. This duty is not limited to citizens. Every person in Australia, whatever their visa or status, must follow Australian law.

The second responsibility is to vote. Once you are a citizen aged eighteen or over, you must vote in federal elections, in state or territory elections, and in any referendum. A referendum is a special vote that asks the people whether to change the Australian Constitution. Voting matters because it is how citizens have a say in who governs them and help to shape the nation's future. Voting is compulsory at the federal and state or territory levels. The booklet adds one detail that is easy to miss: in some states, voting in local council elections may not be compulsory. Voting is unusual because the booklet lists it as both a responsibility and a privilege.

The third responsibility is to defend Australia should the need arise. This does not mean you must join the military. Service in the Australian Defence Force is voluntary. The point is that citizens should be ready to stand together to protect the nation and its way of life if that were ever necessary.

The fourth responsibility is jury service. A jury is a group of ordinary men and women who listen to the evidence in a court case and decide whether a person is guilty or not guilty. Citizens aged eighteen or over who are on the electoral roll can be called to serve, and if they are called they must take part. Jury service is valued because it keeps the court system open and fair, with decisions made by members of the community rather than by officials alone.

When you revise, remember the simple pattern: obey, vote, defend, serve. Each one is something a citizen gives to Australia, and each one appears in the list the booklet calls responsibilities.
keyFacts_en: Citizenship brings additional responsibilities and privileges.
The four responsibilities are to obey the law, vote, defend Australia if needed and serve on a jury if called.
Everyone in Australia, not only citizens, must obey Australian law.
Citizens aged 18 or over must vote in federal, state or territory elections and referendums.
Voting is compulsory in federal and state or territory elections, but may not be compulsory in some local elections.
Service in the Australian Defence Force is voluntary.
A jury is a group of ordinary Australians who decide whether a person is guilty or not guilty.
Citizens on the electoral roll can be called for jury service, which keeps courts open and fair.
guideRef: Part 2 — Responsibilities and privileges of Australian citizenship; Responsibilities

body_en:
The privileges of citizenship are the things Australia gives you in return for your commitment. Part 2 of the booklet lists six of them, and the real test likes to ask which rights belong to citizens alone. A good way to remember them is to think about work, politics, travel, help abroad and family.

The first privilege concerns work. Citizens can apply for jobs in the Australian Public Service, which means working for the Australian Government in places such as Services Australia or the Australian Taxation Office. Citizens can also apply to join the Australian Defence Force, made up of the Army, the Navy and the Air Force.

The second privilege is political. Citizens aged eighteen or over can stand for election to parliament at the federal, state or territory level. There is one important condition: a person who is a dual citizen cannot seek election. The booklet describes serving in a parliament as an honour and a serious responsibility.

The third and fourth privileges concern travel. As a citizen you have the right to live freely in Australia, and you can apply for an Australian passport. If you go overseas, you can come home without needing a visa. This is one of the clearest differences between a citizen and a permanent resident, and it has appeared in the official practice test.

The fifth privilege is consular help. Australia keeps an embassy, high commission or consulate in many countries. If you are overseas and something goes wrong, you can ask an Australian official for assistance. The booklet gives examples such as civil unrest and natural disasters. Officials can also issue an emergency passport and offer advice and support after an accident, a serious illness or a death. The booklet pairs this with a reminder: while you are in another country, you must obey that country's laws.

The sixth privilege is about family. If a citizen has a child who is born overseas, the citizen can apply for that child to become an Australian citizen by descent.

Notice that voting appears on this list as well as on the list of responsibilities. The booklet treats it as both a duty and a right. When a question asks about a privilege, look for something Australia gives you: a passport, a public service or defence job, the chance to stand for parliament, help from an embassy, or citizenship for your overseas-born child.
keyFacts_en: Citizens can apply for jobs in the Australian Public Service and the Australian Defence Force.
Citizens aged 18 or over who are not dual citizens can seek election to parliament.
Citizens can apply for an Australian passport; permanent residents cannot.
A citizen returning from overseas does not need a visa to re-enter Australia.
Citizens overseas can ask Australian officials for help, including an emergency passport.
When in another country you must obey that country's laws.
A citizen can apply for a child born overseas to become a citizen by descent.
guideRef: Part 2 — Privileges

title_en: Taking part, paying tax and the pledge
body_en:
Citizenship is more than a list of rules. Part 2 of the booklet ends by encouraging every citizen to take an active part in Australian life. Active citizens, it says, take on the responsibility and the privilege of shaping the country's future. There are many ways to do this. You might join a neighbourhood or community organisation, volunteer for social or community work, become part of an arts or cultural group, or get involved in political life. A volunteer, in the words of the glossary, is someone who gives their time to a person or organisation without expecting to be paid.

Paying tax is another direct way of contributing, and unlike volunteering it is required by law. Tax is taken from the money you earn, whether that comes from a job, a business or investments, and it is collected by the Australian Taxation Office, usually called the ATO. There are also taxes on many goods and services. The ATO works to make sure that everyone understands their tax rights and obligations and pays the correct amount. The glossary describes the ATO as the agency that manages the tax and superannuation systems.

Why does tax matter? Because it pays for the services Australians rely on: government-funded healthcare and education, defence, roads and railways, and social security. Social security means government pensions and benefits for people who are unemployed, disabled, elderly or otherwise in need. Many of these payments are delivered by Services Australia through Medicare, Centrelink and Child Support. The Australian Government is not the only tax collector. State and territory governments and local councils also raise taxes to fund the services they provide. Together these services help make Australia a peaceful and prosperous country.

The booklet also explains the final step on the path to citizenship. You do not become an Australian citizen when you pass the test or receive a letter. You become a citizen when you make the pledge of commitment at a citizenship ceremony. In the pledge you promise loyalty to Australia and its people, say that you share its democratic beliefs, respect its rights and liberties, and will uphold and obey its laws. The words under God are optional, so each person can choose whether to include them.

A few glossary terms round off this chapter. The Australian Public Service means government departments and the people they employ. Civil unrest means demonstrations and riots by large numbers of people, usually against a government decision. Being self-sufficient means being able to provide for your own needs without relying on others.
keyFacts_en: Active citizens help shape Australia's future by joining community, cultural or political life.
Paying tax is required by law and is collected by the Australian Taxation Office.
Tax is paid on income from a job, a business or investments, and on many goods and services.
Taxes fund healthcare, education, defence, roads and railways, and social security.
State and territory governments and local councils also collect taxes.
You become a citizen when you make the pledge at a citizenship ceremony.
The words 'under God' in the pledge are optional.
Services Australia delivers Medicare, Centrelink and Child Support.
guideRef: Part 2 — Participating in Australian society; A message to you — The Australian Citizenship Pledge; A message to you — The Australian citizenship ceremony; Glossary of testable section

body_en:
Part 3 of the booklet begins with a reminder of the promise you make at the citizenship ceremony: to uphold and obey the laws of Australia. Because Australia is a parliamentary democracy, the booklet says it is important to understand how that system works and how you, as a citizen, will have a say in running the country. The most direct way to have your say is to vote.

Voting starts with enrolment. Australian citizens aged eighteen or over must enrol to vote. Enrolment covers federal elections, state and territory elections, and referenda on changes to the Constitution. Enrolment is not a formality. The booklet states plainly that if you are not correctly enrolled, you are not able to vote. So a new citizen who wants to take part must make sure their enrolment is in place before an election is called.

In a parliamentary democracy, citizens do not run the government themselves. Instead they choose a person to represent them in parliament. When you vote, you are deciding who will speak and act on your behalf, and collectively voters decide who will govern.

Voting in Australia is compulsory. This applies to elections and also to referenda on constitutional change. If you do not vote and cannot give a good reason, you may have to pay a fine. The booklet explains the purpose behind this rule: compulsory voting is a way of making sure that the people, not just a small group, decide who will govern and represent them in parliament.

Although voting is required, how you vote is entirely your own business. Australian elections are conducted by secret ballot, which means you vote privately and nobody can see your choice. The booklet says this leaves you free and safe to vote for any candidate. No one is allowed to know whom you voted for unless you decide to tell them. You cannot be required to reveal your vote to an employer, a party worker, a family member or an official.

The glossary adds a few terms worth knowing. The electoral roll is the list of people registered to vote. An election is the process through which citizens choose their representatives. An electorate is a district of voters who elect a member to the House of Representatives, and electorates are also called electoral districts, divisions or seats. A secret ballot is a system of voting in private so that no one can influence or pressure the voter.

If you remember three things from this lesson, make them these: enrol first, vote because you must, and vote in private because the choice is yours alone.
keyFacts_en: At the citizenship ceremony you pledge to uphold and obey Australia's laws.
Citizens aged 18 or over must enrol to vote in federal, state and territory elections and referenda.
If you are not correctly enrolled, you cannot vote.
Voting is compulsory in Australian elections and in referenda on constitutional change.
Not voting without a good reason may lead to a fine.
Voting is by secret ballot, so you are free and safe to vote for any candidate.
The electoral roll is the list of people registered to vote.
An electorate is a district of voters who elect a member of the House of Representatives.
guideRef: Part 3 — Government and the law in Australia; How do I have my say? — Voting

body_en:
Elections only work if people trust the way they are run. In Australia that trust rests on the Australian Electoral Commission, usually shortened to the AEC. Part 3 of the booklet describes the AEC as a Commonwealth agency with two main jobs. It conducts federal elections and referendums, and it maintains the Commonwealth electoral roll, the list of everyone who is registered to vote.

The booklet stresses one point above all: the AEC is independent of the government. Political parties and people in government cannot influence its decisions. This independence is what makes a fair contest possible. The party in power does not run the election it is competing in, and a minister cannot tell the AEC how to do its work. The glossary explains the word commission as a group of people with an official responsibility, and notes that an independent commission organises the elections.

Voting is not the only way to have your say. Between elections, Australian citizens can contact their elected representative to raise concerns about government policy. A representative, in the glossary's words, is a person who acts or speaks for others. Your local member of parliament is there to listen to the people of the electorate, and through these representatives all Australians can take part in shaping the laws and policies of a government.

The booklet gives a simple example. If a citizen tells their elected representative that a law needs to be changed, the representative should consider what has been suggested. You do not need to belong to a party or hold any special position to do this. Raising a concern with your MP is an ordinary part of democratic life.

Two more glossary terms complete the picture. A referendum is a vote by all voters on a proposed change to the Australian Constitution. Referendums are run by the AEC in the same way as elections, and voting in them is compulsory. An electorate, also called a division or a seat, is the district of voters who elect one member to the House of Representatives, and it is that member who becomes your representative.

Putting the chapter together, there are two channels for your voice. At election time you vote, in secret, for the person you want to represent you, and an independent commission makes sure the process is fair. At any other time you can speak up by contacting that representative directly, knowing that they should give your suggestion genuine consideration. Both channels depend on citizens taking part, which is why the booklet treats enrolment, voting and raising matters with representatives as central to understanding how Australia is governed.
keyFacts_en: The Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) is a Commonwealth agency.
The AEC conducts federal elections and referendums and maintains the Commonwealth electoral roll.
The AEC is independent of the government; parties and politicians cannot influence its decisions.
Citizens can contact their elected representative to raise concerns about government policy.
A representative who is told a law needs changing should consider the suggestion.
A representative is a person who acts or speaks for others.
A referendum is a vote by all voters on a proposed change to the Constitution.
guideRef: Part 3 — How do I have my say? — Voting; How do I have my say? — Raising matters with your representatives; Glossary of testable section

title_en: From six colonies to one nation
body_en:
To understand how Australia is governed today, the booklet asks you to look back to the years before 1901. At that time there was no Australian nation. After British settlement, the continent was divided into six separate colonies, and each of them governed itself. Every colony had its own constitution and made its own laws on matters such as defence, immigration, postage, trade and transport.

This arrangement caused real problems. Moving goods or travelling between colonies was expensive and slow, because each colony had its own rules. Enforcing the law across a border was difficult, since a colony's authority stopped at its edge. And because each colony looked after its own defence, their defence systems were weak. People began to see that the colonies would be stronger if they joined together.

At the same time, something less practical but just as important was happening. An Australian national identity was starting to form. Sporting teams were travelling overseas to represent Australia rather than a single colony. A distinctively Australian culture was growing in popular songs, poems, stories and art. People were beginning to think of themselves as Australians.

Uniting the colonies was a difficult task that took time, but the idea of one nation eventually became reality. On 1 January 1901 the colonies joined together as a federation of states called the Commonwealth of Australia. This event is known as Federation. The glossary describes Federation as the union of colonies into one nation, with the colonies retaining certain powers. That last phrase matters. The colonies did not disappear. They became states, and they kept powers of their own alongside the new national government. This is why Australia today has both a national parliament and state parliaments.

For the test, the date to remember from this section is 1 January 1901. It is the day the colonies became one country and the day the new Constitution took effect. The official practice test asks when the separate colonies joined to become the Australian nation, and the answer is 1901.

In short, the story of Federation has three parts: six self-governing colonies with separate laws, practical difficulties and a growing sense of shared identity that pushed them towards unity, and the creation on 1 January 1901 of the Commonwealth of Australia as a federation of states.
keyFacts_en: Before 1901 Australia was six separate, self-governing British colonies.
Each colony had its own constitution and laws on defence, immigration, postage, trade and transport.
Separate colonies made trade slow and expensive, law enforcement across borders hard, and defence weak.
A national identity was forming through international sporting teams and Australian songs, poems, stories and art.
On 1 January 1901 the colonies united as a federation of states called the Commonwealth of Australia.
Federation means the union of colonies into one nation, with the colonies retaining certain powers.
guideRef: Part 3 — How did we establish our system of government? — Federation; Glossary of testable section

title_en: The Constitution and how it changes
body_en:
The Australian Constitution is the legal document that sets out the basic rules for governing Australia. Its formal title is the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900. The booklet explains that it was originally passed as part of a British Act of Parliament in 1900, and that it came into effect on 1 January 1901. On that day the colonies became one independent nation, the Commonwealth of Australia. The glossary calls the Constitution the supreme law of Australia, the law by which the government itself must abide.

The Constitution created the main institutions of national government. It established the Parliament of the Commonwealth of Australia, which has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate. It also established the High Court of Australia. The High Court has the ultimate power to apply and interpret the laws of Australia, which means it has the final say on what the law means and whether a law is allowed under the Constitution.

A constitution would be of little use if it could never be changed, but it would also be unstable if it could be changed too easily. Australia solves this with the referendum. The Australian people, not the parliament alone and not the courts, decide whether the Constitution is altered. A referendum is a vote by all voters on a proposed change, and voting in it is compulsory.

The booklet gives one example: the 1967 Referendum. In that vote more than ninety per cent of Australians said yes to allowing Aboriginal peoples to be counted in the Census. It remains the best-known successful referendum in Australian history and is the only referendum the booklet names.

Changing the Constitution requires what is called a double majority. Two separate conditions must both be met. First, a majority of voters across the whole nation must vote yes. Second, a majority of voters in a majority of the states must vote yes. Because there are six states, that means at least four states need a yes majority. If a proposal wins the national vote but carries only two or three states, it fails. Equally, if it carries most states but loses the national count, it fails. This rule protects the smaller states from being outvoted by the larger ones and makes constitutional change a genuinely national decision.

The practice test asks what kind of document the Constitution is and what a referendum changes. Remember that the Constitution contains the rules of government, that it can be changed only by the people at a referendum, and that success needs a double majority.
keyFacts_en: The Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900 sets out the basic rules for governing Australia.
The Constitution was passed as a British Act of Parliament and came into effect on 1 January 1901.
The Constitution established the Parliament, with a House of Representatives and a Senate.
The Constitution established the High Court, which has the ultimate power to apply and interpret Australia's laws.
Only the Australian people can change the Constitution, by voting in a referendum.
In the 1967 Referendum more than 90 per cent voted 'Yes' to count Aboriginal peoples in the Census.
A referendum needs a double majority: a national majority and a majority of voters in a majority of states.
guideRef: Part 3 — The Australian Constitution

body_en:
One of the most important ideas in the Constitution is that no single person or group should hold all the power. To achieve this, the Constitution divides the power of government into three separate powers: the legislative power, the executive power and the judicial power. Each is held by a different part of the system, and the booklet says these powers are written into the Australian Constitution itself.

The legislative power is the power to make laws. It belongs to Parliament. Parliament can make new laws and change existing ones, and it is made up of representatives who are elected by the people of Australia. The glossary describes legislative power as the power and authority to make and change the laws. The practice test touches on this when it asks what the parliament does: it makes and changes the laws.

The executive power is the power to put the laws into practice. The glossary calls it the power to administer the laws. The Executive includes the Prime Minister, the Australian government ministers and the Governor-General. The booklet gives the Prime Minister and the Cabinet as its main example. Ministers are each responsible for a government department, and through those departments the laws made by Parliament are carried out day to day.

The judicial power is the power to interpret and apply the law. It is held by judges. When there is a dispute about what a law means, or about whether someone has broken it, judges decide. The booklet makes a point that is often tested: courts and judges are independent of parliament and government. A minister cannot tell a judge how to decide a case, and parliament cannot interfere in a court's ruling. At the top of the court system sits the High Court, which has the final power to apply and interpret Australia's laws.

A simple way to keep the three apart is to think of a law's life. Parliament makes the law, that is the legislative power. The government, led by the Prime Minister and ministers, puts the law into practice, that is the executive power. The courts interpret and apply the law when questions arise, that is the judicial power. Because the three jobs are given to three different bodies, each acts as a check on the others.

Questions on this topic usually ask what each power means or who holds it. Legislative belongs to Parliament, executive to the Prime Minister, ministers and Governor-General, and judicial to judges. And the reason for the division is always the same: to stop one person, or one group, from holding all the power.
keyFacts_en: The Constitution divides government power into legislative, executive and judicial powers.
The division exists to stop one person or group from holding all the power.
Legislative power is the power to make laws and belongs to Parliament, which is elected by the people.
Executive power puts laws into practice and includes the Prime Minister, ministers and the Governor-General.
Ministers are responsible for government departments.
Judicial power is the power to interpret and apply the law, held by judges.
Courts and judges are independent of parliament and government.
The three powers are written into the Australian Constitution.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is the power of government controlled?; Glossary of testable section

body_en:
Australia's Head of State is the King of Australia. This can surprise new citizens, because the person who leads the government day to day is the Prime Minister, not the King. The booklet explains how these two roles fit together, and the explanation begins with the phrase constitutional monarchy.

Australia is a constitutional monarchy. The glossary defines this as a country in which a king or queen is the head of state, but whose powers are limited by the Constitution. The King is Head of State, yet he has to act in accordance with the Australian Constitution. He does not rule in his own right, and he does not have a day-to-day role in government.

Because the King does not live in Australia, his powers are delegated to a representative who does. That representative is the Governor-General. The King appoints the Governor-General on the advice of the Australian Prime Minister. Once appointed, the Governor-General acts independently of all political parties. The official practice test asks whom the Governor-General represents, and the answer is the Head of State, the King of Australia, not a political party and not the Prime Minister.

The same pattern is repeated at state level. In each of the six states there is a governor who represents the King, in a role similar to that of the Governor-General. So the King has one representative for the nation as a whole and one in each state.

Where does the Prime Minister fit in? The booklet says that Australia's system of parliamentary democracy reflects British and North American traditions, combined in a way that is uniquely Australian. In this system the leader of the Australian Government is the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister runs the government, while the King, through the Governor-General, performs the formal and ceremonial functions of a head of state.

For the test, it helps to keep three figures clearly separate. The King is the Head of State, with powers limited by the Constitution and no daily role in governing. The Governor-General is the King's representative in Australia, appointed by the King on the Prime Minister's advice, independent of all parties. The Prime Minister is the leader of the Australian Government. Questions often try to swap these roles, for example by suggesting the Governor-General represents the Prime Minister or that the Prime Minister is the head of state. If you remember that the King is head of state, the Governor-General stands in for the King, and the Prime Minister leads the government, you will be able to answer them.
keyFacts_en: Australia's Head of State is the King of Australia.
Australia is a constitutional monarchy: the King must act in accordance with the Constitution.
The King does not have a day-to-day role in government.
The King appoints the Governor-General as his representative, on advice from the Prime Minister.
The Governor-General acts independently of all political parties.
Because the King does not live in Australia, his powers are delegated to the Governor-General.
In each state a governor represents the King in a role similar to the Governor-General.
The leader of the Australian Government is the Prime Minister.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who is Australia's Head of State?; Constitutional monarchy; Glossary of testable section

body_en:
The Governor-General is one of the most frequently tested figures in Part 3, so it is worth knowing the role in detail. The first thing the booklet says is what the Governor-General is not. The Governor-General is not part of the government. Unlike the Prime Minister and the ministers, the Governor-General does not belong to a party, does not sit in Cabinet and does not make policy. The Governor-General must remain neutral, standing above the contest between parties.

The booklet then lists five duties. The first is signing Bills into law. When both Houses of the Australian Parliament pass a proposed law, called a Bill, it does not become law until the Governor-General signs it. This signature is known as Royal Assent, because the Governor-General gives it on behalf of the King.

The second duty is ceremonial. The Governor-General represents the nation at official occasions and events, performing the formal duties that a head of state would carry out.

The third duty is approving appointments. The Governor-General approves the appointment of the Australian Government and its ministers, including the Prime Minister. The Governor-General also approves the appointment of federal judges and other officials. The booklet makes clear elsewhere that the Prime Minister recommends who the ministers should be; the Governor-General then gives formal approval.

The fourth duty is starting the process for a federal election. Elections are run by the Australian Electoral Commission, but the formal step that sets an election in motion belongs to the Governor-General.

The fifth duty is acting as Commander-in-Chief of the Australian Defence Force. This is a formal position: the Governor-General is the ceremonial head of the Army, Navy and Air Force.

Finally, the booklet mentions that the Governor-General has special powers known as reserve powers. It does not describe them in detail, saying only that they can be used in specific circumstances. For the test, the important point is simply that these powers exist, that they are called reserve powers, and that they are reserved for particular situations rather than used in the ordinary running of government.

When you meet a question about the Governor-General, check it against this list: not part of the government and neutral; gives Royal Assent to Bills; performs ceremonial duties; approves the appointment of the government, ministers, federal judges and officials; starts the federal election process; and is Commander-in-Chief of the Defence Force. Anything that sounds like leading a party, making policy or deciding court cases belongs to someone else.
keyFacts_en: The Governor-General is not part of the government and must remain neutral.
The Governor-General signs Bills passed by Parliament into law; this is called Royal Assent.
The Governor-General performs ceremonial duties.
The Governor-General approves the appointment of the Australian Government, its ministers, federal judges and other officials.
The Governor-General starts the process for a federal election.
The Governor-General is Commander-in-Chief of the Australian Defence Force.
The Governor-General has reserve powers that can only be used in specific circumstances.
guideRef: Part 3 — The role of the Governor-General

body_en:
Australia has three levels of government, and each has its own leaders with their own titles. The booklet gathers these titles into a single table, and the test often asks you to match a title to a role. This lesson walks through the table level by level.

At the top is the Head of State, the King of Australia. The King is represented in Australia by the Governor-General, and in each of the six states by a Governor. Both the Governor-General and the state Governors are representatives of the Head of State; they are not leaders of a government.

The leaders of governments come next. The Prime Minister is the leader of the Australian Government, the national government. A Premier is the leader of a state government, so New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia and Tasmania each have a Premier. A Chief Minister is the leader of a territory government, which is the title used in the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory. A common test trap is to offer Premier when the question is about a territory, or Chief Minister when it is about a state.

Within a government, a minister is a Member of Parliament chosen by a government leader to be responsible for a particular area of government, such as health, education or defence. Ministers are not elected to their ministerial jobs by the public; they are elected to parliament and then chosen by the leader.

The elected members themselves have two titles. A Member of Parliament, or MP, is an elected representative of the people in the Australian Parliament or in a state parliament. A Senator is an elected representative of a state or territory in the Australian Parliament. Both are elected, but a Senator specifically represents a whole state or territory in the Senate.

At the local level, the leader of a local government is the Mayor or, in some areas, the Shire President. A Councillor is an elected member of a local council. Local councils look after the services closest to daily life, and councillors are chosen by the voters of the local area.

To revise, try sorting the titles into three groups. Representatives of the King: Governor-General and Governor. Leaders of governments: Prime Minister for the nation, Premier for a state, Chief Minister for a territory, and Mayor or Shire President for a local council. Elected members: MP, Senator and Councillor, with ministers being MPs who have been given responsibility for an area of government. If you can place any title into the right group and the right level, you can answer the leaders questions with confidence.
keyFacts_en: The Governor-General represents the Head of State in Australia; a Governor represents the Head of State in each state.
The Prime Minister leads the Australian Government.
A Premier leads a state government; a Chief Minister leads a territory government.
A government minister is an MP chosen by a government leader to be responsible for an area of government.
An MP is an elected representative of the people in the Australian Parliament or a state parliament.
A Senator is an elected representative of a state or territory in the Australian Parliament.
A Mayor or Shire President leads a local government; a Councillor is an elected member of a local council.
guideRef: Part 3 — Who are some of Australia's leaders?

body_en:
The national government of Australia goes by several names. The booklet calls it the Australian Government, and notes that it is also called the Federal Government or the Commonwealth Government. All three mean the same thing. The Government is made up of members of the Australian Parliament, and that Parliament has two Houses: the House of Representatives and the Senate. In a federal election, citizens vote to elect representatives to each of these Houses.

The House of Representatives is sometimes called the Lower House or the People's House. To elect it, Australia is divided into federal electorates, and each electorate chooses one Member of Parliament, or MP, who represents the people living there. The number of MPs each state and territory has depends on how many people live in it, so populous states have more members than smaller ones. Overall, the booklet says, there are over 150 members in the House of Representatives. The job of the House is to consider, debate and vote on proposals for new laws or changes to existing laws, and to discuss matters of national importance.

The Senate is the other House. It is sometimes called the Upper House, the House of Review or the States' House. That last name explains how it is built. Every state is represented equally in the Senate, regardless of its size or population.

Each state elects twelve senators, and the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory elect two senators each, giving a total of seventy-six. So a small state like Tasmania has exactly as many senators as a large state like New South Wales. Candidates often report being asked how many senators a territory has, so the figures twelve for a state and two for a territory are worth memorising. Senators, like MPs, consider, debate and vote on new laws and changes to laws, and discuss matters of national importance.

Putting the two Houses side by side shows the logic of the system. The House of Representatives reflects population: more people means more members. The Senate reflects the states: every state has an equal voice no matter how many people live there. Both Houses debate and vote on proposed laws, and both are elected by citizens at a federal election.

For quick revision, remember the alternative names. Lower House and People's House mean the House of Representatives. Upper House, House of Review and States' House mean the Senate. And remember the numbers: over 150 members in the House of Representatives, and seventy-six senators made up of twelve from each state and two from each territory.
keyFacts_en: The Australian Government is also called the Federal Government or the Commonwealth Government.
The Australian Parliament has two Houses: the House of Representatives and the Senate.
The House of Representatives is also called the Lower House or the People's House.
MPs represent the people in their federal electorate, and the number of MPs per state depends on population.
There are over 150 members in the House of Representatives.
The Senate is also called the Upper House, the House of Review or the States' House.
