There are 76 senators: 12 from each state and 2 from each of the ACT and the Northern Territory.
Both Houses debate and vote on proposals for new laws and discuss matters of national importance.
guideRef: Part 3 — How is Australia governed? — The Australian Government; The House of Representatives; The Senate

body_en:
Australia has six states and two mainland territories, and beneath them hundreds of local government areas. Together with the Australian Government these make up the three levels of government. The booklet explains how each level works and what each one does.

Every state has its own parliament and its own constitution, and state governments are based in their capital cities. The leader of a state government is the Premier, while the leader of a territory government is the Chief Minister. State governments operate in much the same way as the Australian Government. In each state a Governor represents the King. In the Northern Territory the equivalent figure is the Administrator, who is appointed by the Governor-General and has a role similar to a state Governor.

There is an important legal difference between states and territories. States have rights recognised by the Constitution and can pass laws in their own right. Territories do not have that protection. The laws of a self-governing territory can be altered or revoked by the Australian Government at any time. In state and territory elections, citizens elect a representative for their area, and those representatives become members of the state or territory parliament.

Below the states sits local government. The states and the Northern Territory are divided into local government areas, which may be called cities, shires, towns or municipalities. The glossary defines a shire simply as a local government area. Each area has its own council, which plans and delivers services for the local community, and citizens in each area vote to elect their local councillors.

The booklet then sets out who does what. Responsibilities sometimes overlap, but in general each level provides different services. The Australian Government looks after taxation, national economic management, immigration and citizenship, employment assistance, postal services and the communications network, social security such as pensions and family support, defence, trade and commerce, airports and air safety, and foreign affairs.

State and territory governments are primarily responsible for hospitals and health services, schools, roads and railways, forestry, police and ambulance services, and public transport.

Local governments, along with the Australian Capital Territory Government, handle the services closest to home: street signs and traffic controls, local roads, footpaths and bridges, drains, parks, playgrounds, swimming pools and sports grounds, camping grounds and caravan parks, food and meat inspection, noise and animal control, rubbish collection, local libraries, halls and community centres, certain child-care and aged-care matters, building permits, social planning and local environmental issues.

Questions on this section usually name a service and ask which level provides it. A useful shortcut: anything national or involving borders and money belongs to the Australian Government; hospitals, schools, police and transport belong to the states; and anything you would see walking down your street belongs to the local council.
keyFacts_en: Australia has six states and two mainland territories; each state has its own parliament and constitution.
A Premier leads a state government and a Chief Minister leads a territory government.
A Governor represents the King in each state; in the Northern Territory an Administrator is appointed by the Governor-General.
States have rights recognised by the Constitution; territory laws can be altered or revoked by the Australian Government.
Local government areas may be called cities, shires, towns or municipalities, each with an elected council.
The Australian Government handles taxation, immigration, defence, social security, trade, airports and foreign affairs.
State and territory governments handle hospitals, schools, roads and railways, police, ambulance and public transport.
Local councils handle rubbish collection, street signs, local roads, parks, libraries and building permits.
guideRef: Part 3 — State and territory government; Local government; What do the three levels of government do?; Glossary of testable section

body_en:
Most of the people elected to Australian parliaments belong to political parties. The booklet describes a political party as a group of people who share similar ideas about how a country should be governed and who work together to have those ideas turned into laws. The glossary adds that parties usually seek to be elected. The main political parties in Australia are the Liberal Party of Australia, the Australian Labor Party, the Nationals and the Australian Greens. Some parliamentarians do not belong to any party, and they are called independents. Joining a party is a free choice; people in Australia may join one if they wish, but nobody is required to.

Parties matter because they decide who forms the government. After a federal election, the Australian Government is generally formed by the party, or coalition of parties, that has the majority of members in the House of Representatives. Note that it is the House of Representatives that counts, not the Senate. The glossary defines a coalition as the joining of two or more political parties, usually to form a government or an opposition. The leader of the party that forms government becomes the Prime Minister, the leader of the Australian Government.

The party or coalition with the second largest number of members in the House of Representatives forms the Opposition. Its leader is called the Leader of the Opposition. The Opposition's role is to scrutinise the government and offer an alternative.

Once a government is formed, the Prime Minister recommends members of the House of Representatives or senators to become ministers. The Governor-General then approves the appointment of the Prime Minister and the ministers. This two-step process, recommendation by the Prime Minister and approval by the Governor-General, is a favourite subject for harder test questions, so keep the two roles distinct.

Each minister is responsible for an area of government known as a portfolio. The booklet gives employment, Indigenous Affairs and the Treasury as examples. The ministers who hold the most important portfolios together make up the Cabinet, which the booklet describes as the key decision-making body of government.

To summarise the chain of events: citizens elect members to both Houses; the party or coalition with a majority in the House of Representatives forms the government and its leader becomes Prime Minister; the second largest group forms the Opposition; the Prime Minister recommends ministers and the Governor-General approves them; each minister takes a portfolio; and the senior ministers form the Cabinet. Knowing this sequence lets you answer almost any question about how Australia's government comes into being.
keyFacts_en: A political party is a group of people who share similar ideas about how a country should be governed.
The main parties are the Liberal Party of Australia, the Australian Labor Party, the Nationals and the Australian Greens.
Parliamentarians who belong to no party are called independents; joining a party is a free choice.
Government is generally formed by the party or coalition with a majority in the House of Representatives.
The leader of the governing party becomes the Prime Minister; the second largest party forms the Opposition.
The Prime Minister recommends ministers and the Governor-General approves their appointment.
A minister's area of government is called a portfolio.
Ministers with the most important portfolios make up the Cabinet, the key decision-making body.
guideRef: Part 3 — What role do political parties play in the way Australia is governed?; How is the Australian Government formed?; Glossary of testable section

title_en: How a Bill becomes law and how courts work
body_en:
Part 3 of the booklet begins with how Australia's laws come into being. The Australian Parliament has the power to make new laws, and to change existing ones, for the benefit of the nation. The starting point is a proposal from a member of Parliament, which is called a Bill.

A Bill travels through both Houses of Parliament. The House of Representatives and the Senate each consider it, debate it and then vote on whether they agree with it. If a majority of members in each House supports the Bill, it is sent to the Governor-General.

The Governor-General signs the Bill, and at that moment it becomes law. This signing is called Royal Assent. The states and territories have their own parliaments, and they make their own laws in much the same way. It helps to remember the order: Bill, both Houses, Governor-General, Royal Assent.

The second half of this lesson covers the courts, which decide what happens when a law may have been broken. Courts in Australia are independent. A court decides whether a person has broken the law and, if so, what the penalty should be, and it may rely only on the evidence placed before it. Inside a courtroom, the judge or magistrate is the highest authority.

A magistrate is simply a judge in a lower court. Judges and magistrates are appointed by the government, but once appointed they are independent. No one can tell them how to decide a case, and the government cannot remove them from their jobs because it dislikes their decisions.

Several protections apply to anyone accused of a crime. A person is treated as innocent until a court finds them guilty. Anyone who appears in court is entitled to have a lawyer represent them. In some cases a court uses a jury, which is a group of ordinary Australian citizens chosen at random from the general population.

The jury's job is to decide whether the accused is innocent or guilty. The judge explains the law to the jury so that its members understand what they must decide. If the jury in a criminal trial returns a guilty verdict, it is the judge, not the jury, who decides the penalty. The glossary describes a criminal trial as a hearing of the facts by a court to decide whether a person is guilty or not guilty of a crime, and a court as a place where legal cases are heard by a judge or magistrate.
keyFacts_en: A proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law is called a Bill.
Both the House of Representatives and the Senate must agree to a Bill by majority.
The Governor-General signs a Bill into law; this is called Royal Assent.
State and territory parliaments make their own laws in a similar way.
Courts are independent and decide cases only on the evidence before them.
The judge or magistrate is the highest authority in a court and cannot be sacked for a decision.
A person is innocent until found guilty, and everyone has the right to a lawyer.
A jury of randomly chosen citizens decides guilt; the judge explains the law and sets the penalty.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws made?; Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The courts; Glossary of testable section

title_en: The police, the AFP and serious crimes
body_en:
The police are the second part of how laws are enforced in Australia. Their role is to maintain peace and order in the community and to protect life and property. Like the courts, the police are independent of the government. If police officers believe someone has broken the law, they can arrest that person and bring them before a court.

The police may give evidence in court, but the decision about guilt belongs to the court alone, never to the police. Australia has several police forces. Each state, and the Northern Territory, has its own police force, which deals with crimes under that state's or territory's laws.

There is also a national force, the Australian Federal Police, usually shortened to AFP. The AFP investigates crimes against federal laws. The booklet's three examples are drug trafficking (the glossary describes this as carrying or buying drugs in order to sell them illegally), offences that threaten national security, and offences that harm the environment.

The AFP has one extra responsibility that is often tested: it carries out general police work in the Australian Capital Territory, which does not have a separate police force of its own. The booklet stresses that the police and the community in Australia have a good relationship.

You can report crimes and seek help from your local police. Bribery of the police is treated very seriously. It is a serious crime to bribe a police officer, and it is a crime even to offer a bribe, whether or not the officer accepts it.

Part 3 then turns to criminal offences. Everyone living in Australia is expected to become familiar with the law, because not knowing a law is no excuse. If you break a law you did not know about, you can still be charged.

The booklet names the most serious crimes. Among them are murder, fraud, assault and sexual assault, armed robbery and theft, violence towards people or their property, possessing illegal drugs, driving a car dangerously, and sexual relations with a child or young person who is under the legal age of consent. The glossary adds that to enforce the law means to make sure people follow it, and that the police enforce the law and keep the peace. If you ever need to report a crime, your local police station is the place to start.
keyFacts_en: The police protect life and property and keep peace and order.
The police are independent of the government.
Police can arrest and bring a person before a court, but the court decides guilt.
Each state and the Northern Territory has its own police force for its own laws.
The Australian Federal Police investigates federal crimes such as drug trafficking, national security and environmental crimes.
The AFP also does general police work in the Australian Capital Territory.
Offering a bribe to a police officer is a crime, even if it is refused.
Not knowing the law is no excuse for breaking it.
guideRef: Part 3 — How are laws enforced? — The police; Part 3 — Criminal offences in Australia; Glossary of testable section

title_en: Domestic violence and the road rules
body_en:
The booklet gives special attention to violence in the home, because some new residents come from places where it is treated differently. In Australia, everyone has the right to safe and positive relationships with family, friends and loved ones. Violence towards another person is illegal and is a very serious crime, and that includes violence inside the home and inside a marriage, which is called domestic or family violence.

Domestic and family violence is wider than hitting. It covers any behaviour, including threats, that is meant to control a partner by making them afraid or putting their safety at risk. The booklet gives examples: hitting, cutting a family member off from their friends and family, and threatening children or pets. None of this is accepted in Australia, and all of it is illegal.

Anyone who commits such a crime can be sent to jail, and this applies equally to men and to women. Nobody has to put up with being harmed or treated badly. When you, or a person you know, are in danger, the right step is to call the police. The glossary repeats that domestic and family violence should be reported to the police.

The final section of Part 3 deals with traffic offences, which are the laws most people meet every day. Road and traffic rules are set by state and territory governments, not by the federal government. Breaking traffic laws can lead to a fine or even a prison sentence. To drive a car in Australia you need two things: a local driver's licence, and a car that is registered.

Everybody travelling in a car must wear a seatbelt, and babies and young children must be placed in an approved car seat. Traffic laws are strict about drugs and alcohol. Driving after taking drugs is illegal, and so is driving with more alcohol in your blood than the legal limit allows. Holding a mobile phone or other device in your hand while you drive is also illegal.

When you study this section, notice how often the booklet pairs a rule with the consequence: a licence and registration to drive at all, seatbelts and car seats for everyone on board, and penalties for drink or drug driving and hand-held phones. Those pairings are the kind of detail a test question is likely to check.
keyFacts_en: Violence in the home or within marriage is called domestic or family violence and is illegal.
Domestic violence includes hitting, isolating a family member, and threatening children or pets.
A man or a woman who commits domestic violence can go to jail.
If someone is in danger, contact the police.
Road and traffic rules are controlled by state and territory governments.
You need a local driver's licence and a registered car to drive.
Everyone must wear a seatbelt, and young children need an approved car seat.
Driving after drugs or over the alcohol limit, or using a hand-held mobile, is illegal.
guideRef: Part 3 — Criminal offences in Australia; Part 3 — Traffic offences; Glossary of testable section

title_en: Rule of law, democracy and freedom of speech
body_en:
Part 4 of the booklet describes the values that every person in Australia is expected to respect, share and uphold. It opens by naming them: freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity. These values are described as central to keeping Australia secure, prosperous and peaceful, and the booklet says they are one of the reasons so many people want to become citizens. Citizenship, it says, means living out these values every day in your local community.

The first point is simple but important: Australian laws apply to everyone in Australia, whatever their background or culture. The first named value is a commitment to the Rule of Law. All Australians are protected by the law and the legal system, and laws are seen as the way a peaceful and orderly society is maintained.

Under the Rule of Law, everyone is equal before the law and no person or group is above it. Everybody is expected to obey the law at all times, and anyone who breaks it will face penalties. The booklet adds a phrase worth remembering: you should follow the law even when no one is watching.

The second value is parliamentary democracy. Australia's laws are made by parliaments that the people elect, which gives citizens a real part in how the country is run. Government power flows from the Australian people, because it is citizens who vote for the people who represent them. Voting is compulsory in Australia, and the booklet treats this as a sign of how important it is to take part in elections.

The third value is freedom of speech. People should be able to express their ideas freely, as long as they stay within the law. They can meet in public or in private to talk about social or political matters, and they can say and write what they think about any topic. Newspapers, television and radio enjoy the same freedom.

Australians are allowed to protest peacefully against the government, because tolerance of peaceful protest is an essential part of democracy. Freedom of speech has limits, though. It is never acceptable to promote violence against a person or group because of their culture, ethnicity, religion or background. It is illegal to make false allegations and illegal to encourage others to break the law.

Finally, respect works both ways: other people's lawful speech and expression must be respected too. The glossary adds that values are the principles that help a person decide what is right and wrong and how to act.
keyFacts_en: Australian values are based on freedom, respect, fairness and equality of opportunity.
Australian laws apply to everyone in Australia, regardless of background or culture.
No person or group is above the law, and you should follow it even when no one is watching.
Laws are made by parliaments elected by the people, and voting is compulsory.
People may express their ideas freely within the law, and the media share the same freedom.
Peaceful protest against the government is allowed and is essential to democracy.
Promoting violence against a group is never acceptable; false allegations and encouraging law-breaking are illegal.
guideRef: Part 4 — Australian values; Part 4 — Our values — Commitment to the Rule of Law; Part 4 — Our values — Parliamentary democracy; Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of speech; Glossary of testable section

title_en: Association, religion and equality under the law
body_en:
The booklet continues with freedom of association. People in Australia may freely choose to join a group, or to leave it, provided the group is lawful. The booklet lists political parties, trade unions, and religious, cultural and social groups as examples.

No one can be compelled to join an organisation, and no one can be forced to leave one. Australians may also gather together, including to protest against something the government or an organisation has done, but every protest has to stay within the law: it must be peaceful, nobody may be injured, and property must not be damaged.

Next comes freedom of religion. Australia has no official national religion, and everyone may follow whichever religion they wish. Whatever a citizen's religion or beliefs, the government treats them the same as anyone else. The booklet then draws a firm line: religious practices must not break Australian law, and religious laws have no legal status in Australia.

Where a religious law differs from an Australian law, the Australian law must be followed by everyone. Two practices are named as illegal. Polygamy, meaning that a person has more than one spouse at once, and forced marriage, which the glossary describes as a marriage where one or both people had no free choice, are both illegal and can bring severe penalties, including prison. Intolerance of other people's religions is not acceptable in Australia, and everyone should have an equal chance to pursue their goals regardless of ethnicity or religion, as long as they obey the law.

The longest section covers equality under the law. Australian society values equal rights for every person, whatever their gender, their sexual orientation, their age, any disability, their religion or race, or their national or ethnic origin, and laws protect people from being treated differently. People from different backgrounds receive neither preferential treatment nor discrimination; the booklet's example is that Buddhists and people of all faiths are treated the same as Christians. Any two people can marry each other, and that includes two men or two women.

Men and women have the same rights and the same access to education and jobs. Both can vote, both can stand for parliament, both can serve in the Australian Defence Force or in the police, and both receive equal treatment in court. Discriminating against someone because of their gender is against the law, and a woman has the right to get a job ahead of a man if she is better qualified and more skilled.

Men and women alike decide personal matters, such as whom to marry and what religion to follow, for themselves, and the law shields them from intimidation and violence. Hitting or otherwise physically harming a spouse or partner is never acceptable and is a criminal offence. Divorce is acceptable, and either spouse may apply to the courts for one, even if the other wants to stay married.
keyFacts_en: People may join or leave any lawful group; no one can be compelled to join or forced to leave.
Protests must be peaceful and must not injure anyone or damage property.
Australia has no official national religion, and religious laws have no legal status.
Polygamy and forced marriage are illegal and can lead to imprisonment.
Religious intolerance is not acceptable in Australia.
Two people can marry each other, including two men or two women.
Men and women have equal rights; a better-qualified woman may get a job ahead of a man.
Violence against a partner is a criminal offence, and either spouse may apply for a divorce.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of association; Part 4 — Our values — Freedom of religion; Part 4 — Our values — Equality of all people under the law; Glossary of testable section

title_en: A fair go, mutual respect and tolerance
body_en:
The last two values in Part 4 are a fair go and mutual respect. The idea of a fair go means that everyone deserves an equal opportunity to succeed and that no one should be held back by class distinctions. Everyone, whatever their background, is given an equal chance to achieve success in life, and making sure that everyone has the same legal rights is described as an important part of fairness. What a person achieves should come from their own hard work and talents.

In practical terms, a job should be won on skills and experience rather than on gender, wealth or ethnic background, and when an organisation fills a position the law supports choosing the applicant with the best skills and experience. The booklet notes that many new migrants have become leaders in business, their professions, the arts, public service and sport through hard work and enterprise.

The final value is mutual respect and tolerance for others. Every individual must respect other people's freedom and dignity, and also their opinions and the choices they make. Being violent towards anyone is against the law, and the booklet stresses that this covers every kind of violence, verbal abuse as well as physical abuse. Australians believe that disagreements should be settled peacefully and, above all, that everyone has the right to be safe, free from violence and free from intimidation.

Two specific points follow. First, Australia's laws on the age of sexual consent are very strict; the age is 16 in some states and territories and 17 in others. The booklet's own example is a 20-year-old man and a 15-year-old girl: a sexual relationship between them is illegal in every state and territory, so it is illegal everywhere in Australia.

Second, the lawful actions of the police should be supported, and a lawful request from a police officer should be obeyed, because all Australians commit to following the law. Mutual respect and tolerance means listening to other people and respecting their views and opinions even when they differ from your own, and being tolerant of one another where you disagree.

The booklet closes this part with a clear statement that racism has no place in Australia. This covers producing or passing on racially offensive material, whether on the internet or in print, and it covers racially abusive remarks made in public, including at sporting events. The glossary explains that racism means prejudice, discrimination, harassment or hatred directed at someone because of their race, colour, or national or ethnic origin, that it is against the law, and that it can be reported to the police or to the Australian Human Rights Commission, an independent body that investigates complaints about discrimination and human rights breaches.
keyFacts_en: A fair go means equal opportunity to succeed, with no limits from class distinction.
Jobs should go to the person with the best skills and experience, not gender, wealth or ethnicity.
Many new migrants have become leaders in business, the arts, public service and sport.
Violence of any kind, including verbal and physical abuse, is illegal.
The age of consent is 16 or 17 depending on the state or territory; a 20-year-old with a 15-year-old is illegal everywhere.
You should obey a lawful request from the police.
Mutual respect means listening to and tolerating views that differ from your own.
Racism has no place in Australia, online, in print, in public or at sporting events.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our values — Equality of opportunity and a 'fair go'; Part 4 — Our values — Mutual respect and tolerance for others; Glossary of testable section

body_en:
The second half of Part 4 turns from values to community, and it begins with the idea of making a contribution. Citizenship gives you the chance to take a full part in the life of the nation, and it means you are ready to carry out your responsibilities as a citizen.

Australians expect everyone living in the country, not just citizens, to participate in society and to contribute to the community. Part of that expectation is practical: everyone has a responsibility to try to support themselves and their families whenever they are able to do so.

The next section is about compassion for people in need, and it introduces a word the test often uses, mateship. Mateship means helping each other in times of need. The glossary adds that it also means receiving help from others, especially in difficult times. The booklet's examples are small and everyday: bringing a cooked meal to an elderly neighbour, giving a friend a lift to a medical appointment, or spending time with someone who is sick, frail or lonely.

Out of this spirit of mateship grows Australia's strong tradition of community service and volunteering, which exists so that people look out for each other and strengthen the community. A volunteer, in the glossary, is someone who gives their time to a person or an organisation without expecting to be paid. The booklet presents volunteering as good for the volunteer as well as for the community. It is a chance to share what you know, to learn new skills, and to deepen both your integration into Australian life and your sense of belonging. There are many opportunities to volunteer across Australia.

The third section covers English. Australian society values English as the national language and as an important element that unites people from many backgrounds. People living in Australia are expected to make an effort to learn it.

The reasons are practical: speaking English helps a person get an education and a job and to integrate more fully into the community, and the booklet calls it essential for economic participation and social cohesion. People who apply for citizenship and whose first language is not English must undertake to make reasonable efforts to learn English.

Note the careful wording: the commitment is to make reasonable efforts, not to be fluent before applying. The glossary ties these ideas together with its definition of integration, which it describes as the process of adaptation by migrants so that they can participate in and contribute to their new and evolving society.
keyFacts_en: Australians expect everyone living in Australia to participate in society and contribute to the community.
Everyone should try to support themselves and their families when they are able.
Mateship means helping each other in times of need, such as taking a meal to an elderly neighbour.
Volunteering strengthens the community and helps the volunteer learn skills and feel they belong.
A volunteer gives their time without expecting payment.
English is valued as the national language and a unifying element of society.
Learning English helps people get an education and a job and integrate into the community.
Citizenship applicants must undertake to make reasonable efforts to learn English if it is not their native language.
guideRef: Part 4 — Our community — Making a contribution; Part 4 — Our community — Compassion for those in need; Part 4 — Our community — English as the national language; Glossary of testable section

title_en: Keeping society safe and loyalty to Australia
body_en:
The booklet's last sections ask what each person can do to keep Australia safe and what loyalty to Australia means in practice. Everyone in Australia shares a responsibility to help protect Australian society. If you suspect that a friend or neighbour is planning to commit a serious crime, you should report it to the Australian government authorities as soon as possible, because that is how the community protects its own safety.

In the same way, anyone who sees or knows about a child being abused should report it to the police so that they can investigate. The booklet then addresses behaviour online. Online abuse, sometimes called cyber abuse, is not accepted in Australia. Its examples are sharing sexual photos or videos online without the other person's consent, stalking someone online, and posting racially abusive remarks about a person.

Many kinds of cyber abuse are against the law. The glossary describes cyber abuse as using technology to threaten, intimidate, harass or humiliate someone with the intention of hurting them, and says it should be reported both to the police and to the online service where it happened. The section on loyalty starts with the citizenship pledge, in which new citizens pledge their loyalty to Australia and its people. The glossary notes that the pledge's phrase from this time forward means from now and into the future.

Loyalty to Australia does not rule out other citizenships. An Australian may also be a citizen of one or more other countries, as long as those countries' laws permit it; this is called dual or multiple citizenship. However, a dual citizen in Australia must follow all Australian laws at all times, and some Australian laws follow citizens overseas.

The booklet's example is that it is illegal for Australians to take part in any sexual activity with a child under 16, whether in Australia or abroad. Australian society rests on a shared obligation not to undermine the country's interests and security. Using social media to share official government secrets would undermine those interests, and promoting distrust and fear of an ethnic community would damage community relations.

The booklet also recalls how Australians come together in a crisis, noting that during the bushfires of 2019 and 2020 many multicultural communities collected money, clothes, food and water for people affected. Part 4 ends by saying that Australia's democratic institutions and shared values have built a peaceful and stable society, that a new citizen becomes part of the nation's story, and that citizenship is our common bond.
keyFacts_en: If you suspect someone is planning a serious crime, report it to government authorities as soon as possible.
If you see or know of a child being abused, report it to the police.
Cyber abuse, such as sharing intimate images without consent or online stalking, is not accepted and often illegal.
In the citizenship pledge, citizens pledge loyalty to Australia and its people.
Dual citizenship is allowed if the other country's laws permit it.
A dual citizen in Australia must follow all Australian laws at all times.
Some Australian laws apply overseas, such as the ban on sexual activity with a child under 16.
Sharing government secrets undermines Australia; promoting fear of an ethnic community damages community relations.
